digest.top_line: Luo T1-2N1 nomogram: PMRT cut 5y LRR 2.2% vs 14.9% (HR 0.164) only in high-risk pts (score >18); no LRR association in low/intermediate risk.
digest.tldr: An all-breast, all-retrospective day on PMRT selection and salvage of post-mastectomy recurrence. Luo and Katz nomograms aim to target nodal and chest wall RT in T1-2N1 / SLN+ disease. They are internally or externally validated, not prospective. Halverson favors entire-chest-wall salvage fields (5-yr CW control 75% vs 36%), but field size is confounded with treatment era.

sites.intro: All five are single-institution retrospective series, several from the pre-taxane, pre-HER2 era. Read the absolute rates as hypothesis-generating for modern risk-adapted PMRT.

studies.name: Close or positive margin after mastectomy and chest wall irradiation (Freedman)
studies.tldr: 8-yr chest wall failure 28% if aged ≤50 vs 0% if >50 (p=0.04) after close/positive margin mastectomy without PMRT, T1-T2, 0-3 nodes.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective review, Fox Chase, 789 mastectomy pts, 1984-1993
🔍 136 (17%) had tumor within 1 cm of the deep margin; 34 met inclusion criteria

details.text: 🔍 Inclusion and baseline
subdetails: Clinical tumor ≤5 cm, 0-3 positive nodes, microscopic margin ≤1 cm, no PMRT
Median age 43 (range 29-76)
Deep margin positive in 2 pts, ≤2 mm in 17, 2.1-4 mm in 7, 4.1-6 mm in 8
65% node-negative, 35% with 1-3 positive nodes; MRM in all

details: 📊 5 chest wall failures; 5- and 8-yr cumulative incidence 9% and 18%

details.text: 📊 8-yr cumulative incidence of chest wall failure by factor
📊 Crude chest wall failure by age

details: 📊 Only 1 isolated chest wall first failure; 3 were associated with distant mets
💊 4 of 5 chest wall failures occurred after adjuvant chemo ± tamoxifen (CMF, CAF, AC era)
⚠️ Age confounded with chemo: 91% of ≤50 got chemo vs 25% of >50
⚠️ 19 of 34 margins never centrally reviewed
⚠️ Age denominators inconsistent within paper: 21/13 in Methods vs 22/12 in Table 1
⚠️ Margin p=0.36 rests on 5 events; underpowered, not evidence that margin is irrelevant

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series, 34 pts, 5 events; age effect confounded by chemo use and rests on a p=0.04 subgroup split. Hypothesis-generating only.
verdict.audience: Post-MRM breast, clinical T1-T2, 0-3 nodes, close/positive deep margin

studies.significance: The margin itself did not separate risk (24% ≤2 mm vs 7% 2.1-6 mm, p=0.36); age did, with 0 of 12 failures above 50. Chemo did not prevent it: 4 of 5 failures followed chemo ± tamoxifen. That puts age, not margin width, at the center of the chest wall RT decision in otherwise low-risk pts.
studies.monday_clinic: In a woman >50 with T1-T2, 0-3 node disease and a close deep margin after mastectomy, this series does not support chest wall RT on the margin alone; it does not extend to tumors >5 cm or ≥4 positive nodes.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** pathology review of 789 pts treated by mastectomy at Fox Chase, 1984-1993. Median follow-up **59 mo** (range 7-143). Cumulative incidence compared by Gray's test.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **34 women** with invasive cancer, clinical tumor ≤5 cm, **0-3 positive nodes**, microscopic deep margin ≤1 cm, and **no postoperative RT**. Median age 43; 21 pts ≤50 and 13 >50 per Methods.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Adjuvant chemo ± tamoxifen in 23 pts (CMF 12, CAF 10, AC 1); tamoxifen alone in 7. Chemo use tracked age: **91%** of women ≤50 vs **25%** of those >50.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5 chest wall failures, median interval 26 mo. **Age was the only factor** that correlated with failure; margin proximity (p=0.36) and T stage (p=0.98) did not. 5-yr OS 82%, DFS 74%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors cite two earlier mastectomy series (Ahlborn, Mentzer) where close margins did not raise local recurrence, both with short follow-up and crude rates only. This series adds the age interaction those series did not report.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents women after MRM with clinical T1-T2 tumors, 0-3 positive nodes and a close or positive deep margin, not irradiated. Does not represent tumors >5 cm, ≥4 positive nodes, or deep muscle involvement.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Age is confounded with chemo receipt, so the two cannot be separated. Most failures were not isolated (3 of 5 with distant mets), and 19 of 34 margins were not centrally reviewed. Pre-taxane, pre-HER2-therapy era systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The title's claim that margin alone is **not an indication** rests on 0 failures in 12-13 older women, a small denominator. The young-age signal is the more defensible finding, and it persisted despite chemo.

studies.interpretation:
The paper's title makes two claims, and they deserve different levels of confidence. The first, that a close or positive deep margin after mastectomy is not by itself an indication for chest wall RT in otherwise low-risk disease, rests on an absence of events: no chest wall failures among women older than 50. With roughly a dozen pts in that group, zero events is compatible with a real risk that is modest but not trivial, and the series simply could not have detected it. The second claim, that women 50 or younger with T1-T2 disease, 0-3 nodes and a margin of 5 mm or less carry a 28% 8-year chest wall failure risk, is the more informative signal, though it too rests on 5 events in 34 pts and a p=0.04 split.

The most important methodological issue is that age and adjuvant chemo travel together here. Nearly every young woman got chemo and only a quarter of the older women did, so the analysis cannot distinguish an age effect from a chemo-selection effect, or from whatever biology prompted the chemo. What it can say is that chemo did not protect: 4 of 5 failures followed chemo with or without tamoxifen. That is consistent with the authors' broader point that systemic therapy in this era did not substitute for local therapy. Readers should still remember these were CMF, CAF and AC regimens, before taxanes, trastuzumab or modern endocrine therapy, and a modern young pt with HER2-positive or triple-negative disease is treated differently.

The margin finding cuts the other way from intuition. Failure was 24% with margins of 2 mm or less versus 7% at 2.1-6 mm, a threefold difference that did not reach significance at p=0.36. With five events, that is a power problem, not evidence of no effect. A reader should not take this paper as showing margin width is irrelevant, only that age carried more of the measurable risk in a very small sample. The failure pattern also matters for an RT reader: only one chest wall failure was isolated, and three came with distant metastases. Some of what chest wall RT would have prevented may not have changed survival, which weakens the case for RT as a survival intervention in this group even where the local risk is real.

The pathology detail is the most transferable lesson. Gross margin assessment was reasonably specific for a close margin but missed 43% of tumors judged 5 mm to 1 cm on gross exam that were 5 mm or less microscopically. That argues for microscopic deep-margin reporting so that young pts at risk are actually identified. The internal inconsistency in age denominators (21 and 13 in Methods, 22 and 12 in Table 1) is small but underlines how fragile the subgroup numbers are.

Against the later randomized PMRT literature and the EBCTCG overview of node-positive disease, this series is a small, older, hypothesis-generating data point. Its durable contribution is that young age belongs in the PMRT discussion for close-margin, low-nodal-burden disease. What would make it wrong is a larger modern cohort showing that risk in young women tracks tumor biology or systemic therapy rather than age itself.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Chest wall failure was 28% at 8 yrs in pts ≤50 vs 0% above 50 without PMRT, while margin width did not separate risk (p=0.36). This supports weighting age over margin distance when deciding on chest wall RT in T1-T2, 0-3 node disease.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Gross margin assessment missed close margins: 43% of tumors judged >5 mm but <1 cm on gross exam were ≤5 mm microscopically. The authors argue for microscopic deep-margin assessment after every mastectomy, especially in young pts, since that is what flags the high-risk group.

open_questions: Does young age predict chest wall failure independent of tumor biology?
Does the margin effect emerge in larger modern cohorts?
Is omission safe in close-margin pts >50 with modern systemic therapy?

studies.name: Isolated local-regional recurrence after mastectomy: radiotherapeutic management (Halverson)
studies.tldr: 5-yr freedom from chest wall re-recurrence 75% vs 36% with large vs small field RT (p=0.0001) for isolated post-mastectomy LRR, no prior PMRT.

details.text: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution series, Mallinckrodt 1964-1986, N=224

details: 🔍 First isolated LRR after mastectomy; prior PMRT, distant mets, and outside-salvage failures excluded

details.text: 🔍 Median f/u 46 mo (range 24-241); actuarial life-table method, timed from recurrence
📊 Whole cohort: 5-/10-yr OS 43%/26%, DFS 25%/15%; 5-yr LRC 57%
📊 Outcomes by site of initial recurrence (5-yr)
📊 Solitary chest wall recurrence: freedom from chest wall re-recurrence by field size

details: ⚠️ Small fields used in only 14 pts, mostly the early era; field size confounded with treatment period
📊 Small-field failures: 33% in-field or at margin, 67% outside field but within chest wall

details.text: 📊 Elective RT to uninvolved sites
📐 Dose: <3 cm recurrences 100% controlled at ≥6000 cGy vs 76% at lower doses
📐 Excised recurrences controlled across 4500-7000 cGy; larger lesions about 50% even at 7000 cGy

details: ⚠️ The SCV OS benefit is an unadjusted retrospective comparison; selection and era effects can explain it

details.text: ⚠️ Late sequelae: G2 9%, G3 1%, no fatal toxicity
subdetails: Arm edema 8/75 (11%) with elective axillary RT vs 1/109 (1%) without
Pneumonitis 2% tangents alone vs 8% (3/37) tangents + parasternal photons
Bone necrosis in 4 pts, all at doses >5400 cGy

details: 🔗 vs Toonkel and Deutsch series cited in source: conflicting survival direction with elective nodal RT, neither reported failure patterns

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective series spanning 2 decades. Field size, dose and elective volumes set by era and physician preference, so the comparisons are confounded. Pre-modern systemic therapy and imaging.
verdict.audience: First isolated LRR after mastectomy, no prior PMRT, no distant mets

studies.significance: The pattern-of-failure detail matters most: two-thirds of small-field failures landed outside the field but inside the chest wall, so the whole chest wall is the at-risk volume. Dose is graded by burden: ≥6000 cGy took <3 cm recurrences to 100% control, while bulky disease plateaued near 50% even at 7000 cGy. Elective axillary RT added arm edema (11% vs 1%) with rare axillary re-recurrence.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with first isolated post-mastectomy chest wall or nodal recurrence and no prior PMRT, this supports treating the entire chest wall plus the uninvolved SCV fossa and leaving the uninvolved axilla out; it does not cover reirradiation after prior PMRT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution review, Mallinckrodt Institute, **1964-1986**, N=224 treated with curative intent. Median follow-up **46 mo** (range 24-241); actuarial survival and failure timed from recurrence.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **First, isolated local-regional recurrence after mastectomy**; excluded any prior PMRT, distant metastases, and pts who failed salvage elsewhere. Chest wall alone 134 (60%), SCV alone 29 (13%); mastectomy radical 34%, modified radical 61%, total 5%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Tangents with 1.5-6.0 MV photons to **4500-5000 cGy**, bolus customary, with a 6-12 MeV electron boost to gross disease. SCV AP field to 4500-5000 cGy at 3 cm; about 90% of treatments at **180-200 cGy/day**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5-yr LRC **57%** overall, and **75%** with adequate-volume RT. Supraclavicular re-recurrence **6% vs 16%** with vs without elective SCV RT (p=0.0489); elective CW RT did not reach significance (17% vs 27%).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G2 sequelae 9%, G3 1%, no fatal toxicity. Arm edema concentrated in elective axillary RT (**8/75, 11%** vs 1/109, 1%); pneumonitis rose with a parasternal field added to tangents (8% vs 2%).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Cited series disagree on elective nodal RT: Toonkel reported a survival advantage with comprehensive nodal RT while Deutsch reported the reverse, and neither gave failure patterns. The small-field failure rate here matches Donegan's excision-alone experience (11 of 15 failing in the chest wall).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents RT-naive pts with a first isolated post-mastectomy chest wall and/or nodal recurrence, no distant mets. Does not represent pts after prior PMRT or salvage failures, or the modern systemic therapy and staging era.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Staging was era-variable (bone scan 64%, abdominal CT 6.3%), so occult M1 disease probably diluted outcomes in early years. Systemic therapy at recurrence (49 chemo, 69 hormonal) was not analyzed against RT alone.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The defensible conclusion is about volume: localized therapy, small field or excision alone, under-treats a chest wall at diffuse subclinical risk. The SCV survival gain and the dose thresholds are hypothesis-generating, since dose was chosen by physician preference.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this series is not its survival numbers, which belong to an era of limited staging and minimal systemic therapy, but its failure-pattern accounting. Halverson and colleagues split the local-regional field into four sites and scored re-recurrence in each, including recurrence in a site that was never involved. That framing is what lets the paper answer a volume question that the survival-focused series it cites could not. Toonkel and Deutsch reached opposite survival conclusions about elective nodal RT without saying where pts failed, so neither could separate a nodal-coverage effect from case selection. Here the failure map points in a clear direction: the chest wall behaves as one at-risk field, the supraclavicular fossa is the nodal site that fails when left untreated, and the axilla and internal mammary chain rarely do.

The large versus small field comparison is the strongest finding and also the most confounded. Small fields came almost entirely from the early period, when the practice was abandoned after the department saw the relapses, so field size travels with era, staging intensity and probably disease burden. What protects the conclusion is the mechanism rather than the p-value. Two-thirds of small-field failures happened outside the portal but inside the chest wall, which a selection explanation cannot easily produce. The concordant excision-alone experience from Donegan supports the same reading: localized therapy leaves subclinical chest wall disease behind.

The nodal findings deserve more caution. The supraclavicular re-recurrence reduction (6% vs 16%) is plausible and agrees with the earlier Bedwinek report from the same institution. The accompanying survival difference (53% vs 35% at 5 years) is an unadjusted comparison in a cohort where elective coverage increased over time, and it should not be read as a survival effect of nodal RT. The toxicity data are what make this useful as a negative recommendation: elective axillary RT carried an arm edema rate of 11% against 1% without it, for a site that seldom failed. The pulmonary signal with parasternal fields points the same way for the internal mammary chain, with the caveat that tangents may have covered those nodes incidentally.

The dose data are graded by burden and are the least generalizable part. Small recurrences controlled completely at ≥6000 cGy, and excised disease controlled across the whole dose range, but the larger and diffuse recurrences sat near 50% control regardless of dose. With dose chosen by the treating physician, a dose-response curve cannot be separated from selection, and the plateau in bulky disease is the more reliable observation: it shows where photon-electron RT alone runs out.

For a modern reader, the series still fits how RT-naive isolated LRR is usually managed, with comprehensive chest wall and SCV coverage and the uninvolved axilla left out. What it cannot settle is the contribution of contemporary systemic therapy, which the authors deferred to a separate analysis, or how results change once modern imaging removes occult M1 disease from the denominator. Its exclusion of prior PMRT also means it has nothing to say about the reirradiation setting.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Two-thirds of small-field failures fell outside the portal but inside the chest wall, which argues for the entire chest wall as the target. Elective SCV RT cut SCV re-recurrence from 16% to 6%, while elective axillary RT added arm edema (11% vs 1%) for a site that rarely failed.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Excision before RT helped: excised recurrences were controlled across 4500-7000 cGy, so the needed dose may come down. The authors reject excision alone, since localized therapy left the rest of the chest wall at risk and chest wall failures continued past 10 years without elective coverage.

open_questions: Contribution of modern systemic therapy to RT for isolated LRR
Does elective SCV RT improve survival after adjustment for era?
Optimal strategy for bulky or diffuse chest wall recurrence

studies.name: Nomogram for ≥4 involved nodes in SLN-positive breast cancer (Katz)
studies.tldr: Seven-factor nomogram predicts ≥4 involved nodes after 1-3 positive SLNs; AUC 0.83 derivation, 0.81 external validation (N=206).
details: 🔍 Retrospective, 2 academic centers (MGH n=248, BWH n=154), N=402 with 1-3 positive SLNs + completion ALND
🔍 Clinically node-negative, no neoadjuvant systemic therapy; ≥6 nodes examined required for inclusion
🔍 External validation: 206 SLN+ pts, Sibley Memorial community hospital

details.text: 📐 Nomogram score components (Fig 2)
subdetails: Primary tumor size (cm) x 2.6
Number of positive SLNs x 9.2
+11 each: LVSI, lobular histology, extranodal extension
+16 if largest SLN met is macrometastasis (>2 mm)
-8.6 if ≥1 SLN negative; constant -58

details.text: 📊 Model performance, derivation vs validation

rows: Could be spared SCV/apex RT at <5% cutoff

details: 📊 At 5% cutoff: 113 of 118 low-risk pts had ≤3 nodes, NPV 94.7%
⚠️ Model somewhat underestimated observed ≥4-node rate in validation set
⚠️ Event count inconsistent: abstract states 87 with ≥4 nodes, Results text states 81
⚠️ Sensitivity reported 97.5%, but stated counts (54 of 57 classified positive) don't reconcile
⚠️ Derived only in dissected pts; the target population (no ALND) was excluded, incl. 73 trial pts given nodal RT
🔗 Builds on MD Anderson model (LVSI, >1 positive SLN, no drainage) and Chagpar model (1,133 SLN+ pts), adds LVSI + met size

verdict.rationale: Retrospective derivation restricted to dissected pts, unlike the undissected pts it targets; internal count discrepancies; validates node-count prediction, not regional control after field reduction.
verdict.audience: cN0 invasive breast, 1-3 positive SLNs, no neoadjuvant therapy

studies.significance: The RT read is the 5% cutoff: 34% and 37% of SLN+ pts fell below it, the group the authors hypothesize could get high tangents instead of a SCV/apex field. The field-related lymphedema numbers the source quotes (2% to 8% rising to roughly 9% to 24%) put a toxicity cost on that nodal coverage decision. Regional control after fields are reduced was never measured.
studies.monday_clinic: In a cN0 pt with 1-3 positive SLNs and no completion ALND, a low nomogram score is evidence for weighing high tangents over a SCV/apex field; it does not extend to post-neoadjuvant pts, who were excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective two-center review (MGH, BWH), **N=402**, with forward stepwise multivariable logistic regression and external validation in **206** community-hospital pts. Presented at ASTRO 2006.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Invasive breast cancer, **clinically node-negative**, **1-3 positive SLNs** on H&E, completion ALND with **≥6 nodes** examined, **no neoadjuvant systemic therapy**. Mastectomy 186 (46%), BCS 215 (53%), median tumor 1.8 cm, ENE in 122 (30%).

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary outcome:** ≥4 total involved axillary nodes (SLN plus non-SLN). Discrimination by AUC, calibration by Pearson and Hosmer-Lemeshow.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Seven independent predictors: tumor size, lobular histology, LVSI, ENE, number of involved SLNs, macrometastasis, and **no uninvolved SLN**. AUC **0.83** in derivation, **0.81** in validation; NPV **94.7%** at the 5% cutoff.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: The paper proposes that pts below **5%** predicted risk might be treated with **modified high tangents** rather than comprehensive nodal RT to the SCV fossa and axillary apex. This is a hypothesis; no RT outcomes were analyzed.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Agrees with the authors' earlier 224-pt series and the MD Anderson model (LVSI, >1 positive SLN). Chagpar's 1,133-pt model used T stage and SLN ratio, and this one adds LVSI and met size. It predates ACOSOG Z0011 and AMAROS, which later reframed whether undissected SLN+ pts need any axillary treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cN0 pts with 1-3 H&E-positive SLNs and no neoadjuvant therapy. Does not represent post-neoadjuvant pts, IHC-only SLN positivity, or pts with ≥4 positive SLNs.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Non-SLNs were read by H&E at **one level**, which may undercount nodal burden. The ≥6-node rule lets some samplings count as dissections, and the stated event count is **87 vs 81** in different sections.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The tool estimates nodal burden; it does not show that treating to that estimate is safe. Whether a low score supports dropping the third field needs regional recurrence data the study lacks.

studies.interpretation:
The nomogram answers a narrow question well and a broader question not at all. It predicts how many axillary nodes would have been found had a dissection been done, and both discrimination and calibration hold up in an external community cohort. It does not tell a radiation oncologist what happens when the supraclavicular and apical fields are dropped on the strength of a low score. That second question is the one the authors raise in the discussion, and the data cannot reach it.

The framing comes from a specific era. In 2008 completion dissection was the standard after a positive SLN, ≥4 involved nodes was the usual trigger for a third field, and a pt without dissection effectively got the RT that would be given to an unstaged axilla. A tool that rebuilds the missing node count fits that logic. Since then ACOSOG Z0011 and AMAROS have made omission of dissection routine in selected pts, and the regional nodal irradiation trials have pushed the indication toward node positivity as such rather than a count of four. So the nomogram's original anchor, the 4-node threshold, matters less today than when it was built, even though the authors already note that some clinicians treat every node-positive pt with regional RT.

Several methodological points should lower confidence in the exact numbers more than the AUC suggests. The derivation cohort is limited to pts who were dissected, while the intended users are pts who were not, and the 73 pts treated on the institutional nodal RT trial without dissection were excluded. If surgeons chose dissection for higher-risk pts, the model was calibrated in a population enriched for nodal burden. Non-SLNs were examined by H&E at one level, which biases toward undercounting. The ≥6-node threshold for calling a procedure a dissection admits some samplings. The internal reporting also does not reconcile: the abstract gives 87 pts with ≥4 nodes and the Results text gives 81, and the stated sensitivity of 97.5% does not match the stated 54 of 57 classified positive. None of these overturns the main result, but a tool meant for individual risk estimates should get its own denominators right.

The validation is a real strength. The Sibley cohort was treated in a different setting, AUC held at 0.81, and goodness-of-fit tests were nonsignificant, although the model somewhat underestimated observed rates there. Underestimation is the clinically dangerous direction for a de-escalation tool, because it is the error that moves pts into the low-risk bin.

For current practice the most transferable piece is the set of predictors rather than the score: macrometastasis, ENE, LVSI, lobular histology, multiple positive SLNs and no negative SLN together describe the undissected axilla most likely to hold residual disease. The 5% cutoff, which placed 34% and 37% of pts in a low-risk group, is a reasonable starting point for a prospective question, not an answer to it. A trial of field reduction guided by this score, with regional recurrence and lymphedema as endpoints, would settle what the paper can only propose.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: At the 5% cutoff, 34% and 37% of SLN+ pts were low risk, the group proposed for high tangents without a SCV/apex field. The source cites lymphedema rising from 2% to 8% to roughly 9% to 24% with that field, but regional control after field reduction was not studied.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Seven pathologic factors (macromet, ENE, LVSI, lobular, number of positive and negative SLNs, tumor size) estimate residual axillary burden without completion ALND. NPV was 94.7% at the 5% cutoff, but the model was derived only in dissected pts and does not apply after neoadjuvant therapy.

open_questions: Does nomogram-guided omission of SCV/apex RT preserve regional control?
Calibration in undissected SLN+ pts treated after Z0011

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective; risk cutoffs derived and tested in the same data, no external validation; PMRT assigned by clinician choice, so confounding by indication.
verdict.audience: T1-2N1 breast, mastectomy + ALND, no neoadjuvant therapy

studies.significance: The low-risk unirradiated group (score ≤10) ran 5y LRR 0.4%, the strongest omission signal here, while intermediate-risk pts sat at 6.1% with a non-significant PMRT association on few events. Fields covered chest wall plus supraclavicular/infraclavicular nodes at 46-50 Gy, so any benefit is for comprehensive PMRT, not chest wall alone.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1-2N1 pts after upfront mastectomy and ALND carrying T2, 3 nodes, ER-negative, grade III and LVI, this supports comprehensive PMRT; it does not establish omission as safe in intermediate-risk pts, nor apply after neoadjuvant therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** cohort, mastectomy 2001-2012, median follow-up **74.9 mo**. Fine-Gray nomogram for LRR built in **623 unirradiated** pts; decision-tree cutoffs (score **10 and 18**) defined three risk groups; PMRT effect tested within each.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **T1-2, 1-3 positive axillary nodes**, mastectomy with negative margins and ALND; neoadjuvant therapy and synchronous metastases excluded. All pts got adjuvant chemo, 90.5% anthracycline- or taxane-based; median age 47.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: CT-planned EBRT **46-50 Gy in 23-25 fx** to chest wall, infraclavicular and supraclavicular regions. IMN added for central tumors, axilla only with ECE.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Nomogram C index **0.73** (0.68-0.78). PMRT associated with lower LRR only in the **high-risk** group (P<.001); not in low (P=.930) or intermediate (P=.240) risk.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors frame against **EBCTCG**, where control-arm 10y LRR in 1-3 nodes was **21%**, far above this cohort's 6.0% 5y LRR without PMRT. They defer to **SUPREMO** and **NSABP B-51** for prospective answers, the latter for the post-neoadjuvant setting this study excludes.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-2N1 breast cancer after upfront mastectomy with negative margins and ALND, treated with adjuvant chemo. Does not represent pts after neoadjuvant therapy or staged without ALND.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cutoffs fitted and evaluated on the same data invite optimism; the nomogram lacks external validation. Nodal size and margin width were unavailable, and HER2+ pts were largely untreated with trastuzumab.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The high-risk translation of a **12.7%** 5y LRR gain into a **7.0%** BCM gain mirrors the EBCTCG local-control-to-survival ratio the authors cite. What it does not settle is whether intermediate-risk pts, with 6.1% baseline LRR, can safely omit PMRT.

studies.interpretation:
The question this paper addresses is the oldest unresolved one in PMRT: which T1-2N1 patients need it now that contemporary systemic therapy and more thorough axillary surgery have pulled baseline locoregional risk well below the 21% control-arm rate the EBCTCG meta-analysis was built on. This cohort's unirradiated 5-year LRR of 6.0% sits in the modern range the authors cite, which is exactly why a blanket PMRT recommendation drawn from EBCTCG feels overextended to many readers. The authors' answer is a five-variable score (T stage, 3 vs 1-2 nodes, ER, grade, LVI), and the variables are unsurprising; the interest lies in the stratification.

The most defensible finding is not the high-risk benefit but the low-risk floor. Unirradiated pts scoring ≤10 had 5-year LRR of 0.4%, a rate at which no plausible relative reduction from comprehensive nodal RT would offset cardiac and pulmonary exposure. That finding depends only on the natural history arm and is less exposed to treatment-selection bias than any PMRT comparison here.

The high-risk benefit (HR 0.164 for LRR, with DR and BCM moving in parallel) deserves more caution than its p-values suggest. PMRT was a clinician choice, applied preferentially to younger pts, larger tumors and more nodes, and multivariable Fine-Gray adjustment cannot remove confounding by indication or unmeasured factors such as nodal size and margin width, which the authors acknowledge they lacked. The cutoffs of 10 and 18 were selected by a decision tree on the same unirradiated pts whose outcomes then define the groups, so the separation between strata is optimistic by construction. A bootstrap C index of 0.73 is respectable but internal; without an independent cohort, the thresholds should be read as one institution's partition, not a portable rule. The overall DR figures (16.6 vs 17.8% alongside HR 0.608) also read inconsistently in the source, which nudges confidence in the reporting down a notch.

The intermediate group is where the clinical difficulty actually lives, and the paper is least able to help there. Baseline LRR of 6.1% with P=.240 for PMRT on few events is an underpowered null, not evidence of equivalence. The authors say as much. A reader tempted to use this score to omit PMRT in an intermediate-risk patient is extrapolating beyond what 13 versus 6 events can carry.

Transferability is further limited by era and regimen: trastuzumab reached only 26.2% of HER2+ pts, all pts were staged by ALND (median 17 nodes dissected), and anyone receiving neoadjuvant therapy was excluded. The RT technique, 46-50 Gy to chest wall and supraclavicular/infraclavicular nodes with selective IMN coverage, is conventional and transferable, but the systemic and surgical context is not today's. For a radiation oncologist, the paper is most useful as support for omission in the clearly low-risk tail and for comprehensive PMRT when adverse features cluster, while the middle remains a question for randomized data such as SUPREMO rather than for this nomogram.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The low-risk unirradiated group (score ≤10) ran 5y LRR 0.4%, the strongest omission signal, while intermediate-risk pts sat at 6.1% with an underpowered null. Benefit in high-risk pts came with comprehensive fields at 46-50 Gy including supraclavicular/infraclavicular nodes, not chest wall alone.

open_questions: External validation of the nomogram in an independent cohort
PMRT benefit in intermediate-risk T1-2N1 disease
Role of PMRT after neoadjuvant therapy

studies.name: Chest wall recurrence outcomes by initial stage and PMRT implications (Chagpar)
studies.tldr: After CWR without prior PMRT, 5-yr OS 79.9% (T1-T2N0) vs 41.9% (T1-T2, 1-3 LN+) vs 29.1% (T3-T4/>4 LN+); 1-3 LN+ salvage no better than advanced.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective review (MDACC), CWR evaluated 1988-1998, N=96
🔍 All pts had mastectomy without PMRT; no distant mets at time of CWR

details.text: 🔍 Groups by initial stage
subdetails: Group 1: T1-T2N0, n=41
Group 2: T1-T2 with 1-3 positive LN, n=20
Group 3: T3-T4 or >4 positive LN, n=35

details.text: 📊 5-yr outcomes after CWR by initial stage group
📐 Cox MVA for OS, pairwise group comparisons

details: 📊 No XRT for CWR independently predicted worse OS: OR 4.524 (95% CI 2.064-9.918), p<0.001
📊 No XRT for CWR also predicted worse DMFS: OR 4.024 (95% CI 1.825-8.874), p=0.001
📊 Interval to CWR ≤24 mo predicted worse OS: OR 4.636 (95% CI 2.106-10.206), p<0.001
⚠️ Group 2 n=20; the Group 2 vs 3 null comparison is underpowered, not evidence of equivalence
⚠️ XRT-for-CWR benefit confounded: some pts were not irradiated because of progression on systemic therapy
⚠️ Internal inconsistencies: DMFS pairwise ORs in text repeat the OS ORs; Group 2 vs 3 DMFS p given as 0.250 and 0.492
⚠️ Group 3 pts did not get PMRT despite it being standard (refusal, physician bias, often unknown): selected cohort
🔗 Pre-taxane, pre-HER2-targeted era; salvage rates may not transfer to modern systemic therapy

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series, n=20 in the key 1-3 LN+ group; PMRT benefit inferred indirectly from salvage outcomes, not measured. Selection into the no-PMRT cohort unexplained.
verdict.audience: Post-mastectomy breast cancer, no PMRT, isolated chest wall recurrence

studies.significance: The RT signal sits in two places: salvage after CWR in T1-T2 with 1-3 positive nodes was as poor as in T3-T4/>4 LN+ (Group 2 vs 3 OR 1.544, p=0.330), and omitting XRT for the recurrence itself carried OR 4.524 for death. Prevention of CWR, not reliance on salvage, is the argument for PMRT in 1-3 LN+ disease.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1-T2 tumors with 1-3 positive nodes after mastectomy, this supports counting poor post-recurrence salvage when weighing PMRT; it does not argue for PMRT in T1-T2N0 disease, where salvage outcomes after CWR were favorable.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** review at MDACC of CWR evaluated 1988-1998. Of 155 pts identified, 25 with distant mets at CWR and 34 with prior PMRT were excluded, leaving **N=96**. Median follow-up from CWR 41.4 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pathologically confirmed CWR after mastectomy, **no prior PMRT**, no concomitant distant mets. Group 1 T1-T2N0 (n=41), Group 2 **T1-T2 with 1-3 positive LN** (n=20), Group 3 T3-T4 or >4 positive LN (n=35).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: XRT was part of CWR treatment in 29 (70.7%), 15 (75.0%) and 24 (68.6%) pts by group. Dose, fractionation and target volume for salvage RT not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: OS and DMFS measured from the date of CWR, Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, Cox regression for multivariate analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Group 1 outperformed Groups 2 and 3, while **Group 2 vs 3 showed no difference** (MVA OS OR 1.544, p=0.330). **No XRT for CWR** remained adverse in MVA for OS (OR 4.524) and DMFS (OR 4.024).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The randomised PMRT trials the authors cite (the Danish and British Columbia trials) enrolled 1-3 LN+ pts and showed an OS benefit; this series supplies the salvage-failure arm of that argument. SUPREMO later tested PMRT directly in intermediate-risk disease.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents mastectomy pts not given PMRT who develop isolated CWR without distant disease. Does not represent pts with prior PMRT, synchronous distant mets, or modern taxane/HER2-targeted systemic therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Text reports identical ORs for OS and DMFS pairwise comparisons and two different Group 2 vs 3 DMFS p-values, suggesting reporting errors. The Group 3 no-PMRT cohort reflects refusal and physician bias, an unrepresentative slice of high-risk disease.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: If salvage after CWR fails as often in 1-3 LN+ disease as in high-risk disease, the absolute OS value of PMRT depends mostly on baseline LRR risk and toxicity, not rescue. The study does not measure that LRR risk or any PMRT effect directly.

studies.interpretation:
The PMRT argument for T1-T2 tumors with one to three positive nodes has always rested on three quantities: the locoregional recurrence risk without radiation, the toxicity of treatment, and how well a recurrence can be rescued. The randomised trials answered the first two in their own populations, and opponents of routine PMRT leaned on the third, reasoning that a chest wall recurrence in intermediate-risk disease could be caught and salvaged. This series attacks that third premise. Among pts never given PMRT who developed isolated chest wall recurrence, the 1-3 node-positive group did no better after salvage than the T3-T4 or more-than-four-node group, with 5-yr OS of 41.9% vs 29.1%, and the multivariate Group 2 vs 3 comparison was null (OR 1.544, p=0.330). Node-negative pts, by contrast, did well after salvage (5-yr OS 79.9%).

The central inference deserves skepticism on statistical grounds. Group 2 contains only 20 pts, and the confidence interval for the Group 2 vs 3 comparison runs from 0.645 to 3.699. That interval is compatible with meaningfully better salvage in Group 2; the study shows the groups were not distinguishable, not that they were equivalent. The direction of the finding is plausible biologically, since node-positive recurrence likely signals occult systemic disease, but the data cannot carry an equivalence claim.

The cohort itself is unusual. Every Group 3 patient missed PMRT that was standard at the time, through refusal, physician bias, or reasons the authors could not reconstruct. Such pts may differ from typical high-risk disease in comorbidity, adherence, or tumor features, and that bias could push Group 3 outcomes in either direction. The era also matters: treatment predates taxane standardisation and HER2-directed therapy, and modern systemic therapy may rescue both chest wall recurrence and the micrometastatic disease behind it more effectively, which would narrow the stakes of a recurrence.

The secondary finding that omitting XRT for the recurrence predicted worse OS and DMFS is the most radiation-specific result, and the most confounded. Pts not irradiated included those progressing on systemic therapy and those treated with palliative intent, so the radiation variable partly encodes disease biology. It supports RT as a component of CWR salvage but does not isolate its effect.

There are also reporting problems: the pairwise DMFS odds ratios in the text duplicate the OS odds ratios exactly, and the Group 2 vs 3 DMFS p-value appears as both 0.250 and 0.492. These lower confidence in the precise estimates without overturning the qualitative pattern. The study's lasting contribution is conceptual: for intermediate-risk disease, prevention of chest wall recurrence matters because rescue is unreliable. Whether PMRT delivers an OS benefit in that population was a question for SUPREMO and later meta-analytic work, not for a 96-patient salvage series.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Salvage after CWR in T1-T2 with 1-3 positive nodes matched the T3-T4/>4 LN+ group (5-yr OS 41.9% vs 29.1%), weakening the 'watch and salvage' position against PMRT. XRT as part of CWR treatment independently tracked with OS (OR 4.524), supporting RT as a standard component of salvage.

open_questions: Does salvage after CWR remain poor for 1-3 LN+ pts with modern systemic therapy?
Does PMRT improve OS in T1-T2 with 1-3 positive nodes?
What does XRT add to CWR salvage when controlled for disease progression?

papers.title: Nomogram Predicting Locoregional Recurrence to Assist Decision-Making of Postmastectomy Radiation Therapy in Patients With T1-2N1 Breast Cancer
Nomogram for the Prediction of Having Four or More Involved Nodes for Sentinel Lymph Node–Positive Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Purpose The standard of care for patients with a positive (+) sentinel lymph node (SLN) is axillary dissection; however, for various reasons, some SLN+ patients do not undergo dissection. The purpose of this study was to define possible predictors of having four or more involved nodes to provide information for clinicians and patients making decisions about adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation. Patients and Methods We reviewed the records of 402 patients with invasive breast cancer and one to three involved SLNs who underwent completion axillary dissection at two academic cancer centers. None of these patients received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Factors associated with having four or more involved axillary nodes (SLNs and non-SLNs) were evaluated by univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis. Results Eighty-seven patients had four or more positive nodes. On multivariate analysis, having four or more SLNs was associated with tumor histology, primary tumor size, lymphovascular space invasion, extranodal extension, the number of involved SLNs, the number of uninvolved SLNs, and the size of the largest SLN metastasis. A nomogram to predict the probability of having four or more nodes based on patients’ pathologic data was developed from the multivariate logistic regression model. A separate previously published data set of 206 SLN+ patients treated at a community hospital in another city was used to validate this model. Conclusion Patients with a low probability of having four or more nodes can be identified from known pathologic features. The nomogram developed will be helpful to clinicians making adjuvant treatment recommendations.
